Modern large language models generate text one token at a time, with each new token depending on all previously generated tokens. This autoregressive paradigm presents a fundamental computational challenge: at each generation step, the model must process the entire context history to predict the next token. Without optimization, the computational cost grows quadratically with context length—processing 4,096 tokens requires sixteen times the compute of processing 1,024 tokens, making truly long-context applications impractical.

## The Core Challenge in autoregressive models

When large language models generate text, they process tokens one at a time, with each new token depending on all previous tokens in the sequence. In the transformer architecture, this dependency is computed through attention mechanisms where every token attends to every other token to determine relevance. For a sequence of length *n*, this requires computing attention scores between all pairs of tokens—a quadratic operation that becomes computationally expensive as sequences grow.

During inference, the model must calculate key and value vectors for each token position. These vectors encode positional and semantic information that enables the model to understand context. The critical inefficiency arises because when generating token *n+1*, the model must recompute key and value vectors for all previous *n* positions, even though these computations were already performed when generating tokens 1 through *n*. This redundant computation creates a significant bottleneck for processing long sequences.

Rather than recomputing these vectors for every new token generation, the model retrieves them from cache and only computes the vectors for the newly generated token. This transforms the attention computation from a quadratic operation across the entire sequence into a linear operation where new tokens attend to the cached historical keys and values.

Without optimization, this means that generating the 100th token requires computing attention over 99 previous tokens, the 101st token over 100 tokens, and so on.
